title: Propose an Observation
subtitle: Design a survey for a stated goal, predict what it will find, check it against the model and justify the plan: many plans are right
body:
Step 1 of 4 read

The brief

You have ten nights. Find sources of the flattened class (counts rising by 0.4 dex a magnitude) to a depth of 22.5 magnitude, over at least 100 square degrees, with at least 95 percent of the detections real. Three facilities are on offer: the Las Cumbres 0.35 m and 1.0 m telescopes and Rubin. Use the panel to explore, then propose one plan.

There is no single right plan. The check is whether your plan meets the goal and whether what you say it reaches matches it.

title: Propose an Observation
subtitle: Design a survey for a stated goal, predict what it will find, check it against the model and justify the plan: many plans are right
body:
Step 4 of 4 read

Many plans, one goal

The one-meter telescope with about 60 s a visit for ten nights, Rubin with about 30 s, and the 0.35 m telescope with about 1000 s all meet this goal; a threshold of 3 sigma deepens each but fails the reliability. The screen judges feasibility and consistency, never one answer. The count’s interval is Poisson only: a real survey scatters more, from clustering and from the real population differing from a stated class.

title: Propose an Observation
subtitle: Design a survey for a stated goal, predict what it will find, check it against the model and justify the plan: many plans are right
body:
Step 6 of 7 question

What the interval misses

The panel gives a count with a Poisson interval.

Which effect makes a real survey’s count scatter more than that interval?

A Poisson count assumes sources fall independently. Real sources cluster, so the variance between fields is larger, and a survey should state its interval with that included.
